overview: The Duchy of Modena and Reggio was an Este-ruled state in northern Italy, with Modena as its capital after the loss of Ferrara in 1598. This imported 1650 to 1815 record is only a rough guide: its outline extends too far north toward Mantua, and the continuous date range hides the interruption of ducal rule from 1796 to 1814. The restored duchy survived well beyond 1815, ending in 1859.

sections.title: A capital rebuilt around a court

items.text: In 1598, before this map interval, the Este rulers lost Ferrara to the papacy and moved their capital to Modena. They retained Modena, Reggio and Garfagnana. The new capital inherited court collections, administrative traditions and a dynasty whose ambitions were larger than one city.

The restoration of 1814 did not simply switch an old government back on. Francesco IV issued a plan of government on 28 August, organizing centralized institutions under the ruler’s personal control. Records from these ministries survive, showing how a small duchy managed finance, education, diplomacy and internal affairs.

Modena had an inland port. Francesco I’s Darsena began operating around the middle of the seventeenth century, and in 1667 sloping loading areas were added so carts could reach the water’s edge. Heavy goods could travel by boat before continuing their journey on wheels.

Canals powered mills and machinery used for spinning and making paper. Washwomen cleaned clothes in spring-fed channels and spread them on meadows outside the walls. Water was a workplace as well as a route for travelers: the same city needed laundry, flour, cloth and transport.

Wells supplied drinking water to homes, courtyards and public fountains. The city’s coat of arms even shows two crossed drilling tools, honoring the skill of reaching groundwater. A detailed city plan drawn by Giovanni Battista Boccabadati in 1684 records canals and underground drains, helping us reconstruct this watery landscape.

sections.title: What does your patient do for a living?

items.text: Bernardino Ramazzini taught medicine in Modena from 1682 and published his study of workers’ illnesses in 1700. He treated occupation as a serious clue when investigating disease. The health of people who earned their living with their hands belonged in medical scholarship too.

Writing sample: the Latin title of Ramazzini’s 1700 Modena book is “De morbis artificum diatriba,” meaning “A discussion of the diseases of workers.” The University of Iowa preserves and catalogs this edition, printed by Antonio Capponi. Latin let scholarly readers in different countries share a medical argument.

In the expanded version of his treatise, published after he moved to Padua, Ramazzini connected stoneworkers’ dust with breathing problems and described irritation suffered by laundry workers. He considered both harmful substances and awkward bodily movements. These observations concern several occupations and places, not a survey proving that every Modenese worker had the same illness.

sections.title: Schools, care and a garden with a purpose

items.text: University teaching was renewed in Modena in 1682 with subjects including philosophy, medicine, law and theology. Municipal resources and donations helped support it. In 1772, ducal reform placed the university under direct state control and funding, connecting advanced education more closely to government needs.

Part of the new hospital opened on 30 November 1758. The duke commissioned medals to place in its foundations, turning the building itself into a message for the future. The surviving complex reminds us that eighteenth-century urban improvement included places intended for treating illness.

The Albergo dei Poveri, built between 1764 and 1771, combined support for destitute people with work. In 1788 it became the Albergo delle Arti. These names describe an institution that joined charity, training and labor; they should not be mistaken for an ordinary hotel where guests booked a holiday.

In 1758, the duke set aside part of his court garden for medicinal plants. A public botany chair followed, and the garden came under university administration in 1772. Beds of useful plants surrounded a central pool that supplied irrigation and held aquatic species. This garden was a living classroom.

ending.text: The duke left Modena in June 1859, and provisional governments replaced the Austria-Este administration. The state archive preserves the assembly’s decrees ending the dynasty and seeking union with Sardinia. The duchy’s end belonged to Italian unification, not to the imported map cutoff of 1815.
